title: Server-side tools: search, code execution, and web fetching

opening.headline: When it is too burdensome to implement searches and calculations yourself, we will find out what server tools the provider runs on your behalf and when to use them.
body: Search integration is required to provide up-to-date answers, and a secure code execution environment is required to make accurate calculations. If you manually extract web page text or process PDFs, not only implementation but also subsequent maintenance will be a huge burden.

In this class, we will look at the differences between the tools run by the app and the tools run by the provider server, the types of server tools provided by the three companies, web search and grounding, web fetch and code execution, and the structure of tool costs. Next, we use a case study to check the flow of server tool intervention and the decision to choose between direct implementation and provided tools with less burden of change.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the types and roles of server tools run by the provider
You can decide which has the least burden of change between direct implementation tools and provided tools.

screens.title: It is a burden to make searches and calculations yourself.
screens.lead: Assuming you're creating a feature yourself, read on to see what comes next. Let's take a look at how much work this seemingly simple function holds.

visual.alt: A side-by-side view of a checklist of items that need to be implemented and an estimated effort bar.
labels: The work doesn't end even after implementation

paragraphs: Let's say we want the model to base its answers on the latest information. You must write your own code to link the search API, refine results, and organize sources. You also need to decide which results to pass on to the model and how to indicate the source.

The problem becomes even bigger if precise calculations are required. You need to set up a separate, secure sandbox to run the code produced by your model. Extracting the text of web pages and processing PDFs also require separate implementations.

It's not over even after implementation. If the structure of the search target site changes or the linked API changes, the code must be continuously updated. What if there was a tool that would allow providers to take on this burden? The question in this class is what the tool is and under what conditions it is appropriate to use it.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which will last longer: the cost of creating a feature or the cost of maintaining it once created? Answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Before we move on to the fact that there are tools that providers do for you, let's first think about your own experience.

screens.title: think about it
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a situation where the model responded “I don’t know the latest information”?
items.answer: The model only knows up to the time it was trained and what is contained in this request. If you need the latest information, you have to get it from outside, and a search tool plays that role.

items.prompt: Have there been instances where the model made a calculation mistake and gave a plausible answer?
items.answer: The calculations may be incorrect because the model creates text that looks like numbers rather than calculating the numbers directly. For calculations that must be accurate, it is safer to use the results obtained by running the code. The code execution tool takes care of this.

items.prompt: Have you ever spent time maintaining external service integration code?
items.answer: Whenever the integration target changes, my code is affected. The burden of maintenance extends beyond the initial implementation. Who to entrust this burden to is an important criterion in tool selection.

screens.outro: I will summarize my experience with the concept of server tools. First, we look at who is running the tool.

screens.title: What are server tools: who runs them?
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the flow changes when the person running the tool changes.

visual.alt: Two flowcharts comparing who executes and the number of round trips for client tools and server tools.

states.label: client tools
states.body: When the model requests the call, my app runs the tool and returns `tool_result`. The execution environment, permissions, error handling, and retries are all the responsibility of my app. This approach is necessary for things the provider does not know, such as when dealing with internal data or company-specific rules. Instead, your app must implement the round trip itself and create the actual behavior of the tool yourself.

states.label: server tools
states.body: Server tools (`web_search`, `web_fetch`, `code_execution`, `tool_search`) run on Anthropic infrastructure. There is no need for the app to return `tool_result` because the results are carried in the same response. Gemini's built-in tools (Google Search, Maps, Code Execution, URL Context, File Search) are also executed by Google servers within a single API call. However, when mixing it with a function you created yourself, the step of returning the client tool result may be required again.

When moving code, correspond based on function rows, and check each company's usage method in the corresponding documentation. Even if the name is the same, the behavior may differ if the version value is different. For example, Claude's web search has three versions: web_search_20250305, web_search_20260209, and web_search_20260318. A column in the table that is not covered does not mean that the function does not exist, but that it was not used as a subject of comparison in this class.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at how each tool works in practice, one by one. First, web search.

screens.title: Web search tools and Search grounding
screens.lead: Walk through step-by-step how a web search tool works within a request. Select the right arrow to follow from the search query to the cited answer.

visual.alt: Web search step flow: querying a search, receiving results, filtering, citing answers, and answers with sources.
labels: 1 Create a search query (the model determines when)
3 Dynamic filtering (filtered in code and put into context)
Can be repeated multiple times within one request

steps.title: 1. Decide when the model will search
steps.body: With Claude's Web Search, the model sees prompts and decides when to search. It doesn't always search just because you turn the tool on; it searches when it determines it's needed. Execution is handled by the API, and you can set an upper limit on the number of searches per request with `max_uses`. According to the document, simple factual questions are usually searched 1 to 3 times, while comparative or multi-target investigations are searched 10 or more times.

steps.title: 2. Run the search and receive results
steps.body: The API performs a search, which may be repeated multiple times within a single request. If the first results are insufficient, change the query and search again. Apps do not need to implement this iteration.

steps.title: 3. Dynamic filtering
steps.body: `web_search_20260209` and later versions support dynamic filtering, which filters results by code and puts them into context, and can be used in Claude 4.6 and later models. Reduces tokens by leaving only the parts you need instead of dumping the entire search result into context.

steps.title: 4. Answer with quotation
steps.body: The response includes a citation based on the search results. Users can check the sources to support their answers. Gemini's Google Search grounding also increases realism and provides sources with real-time web information.

steps.title: 5. Three ways of OpenAI
steps.body: OpenAI's web search has three types: a quick search type, an agent type where an inference model drives the search, and an in-depth research type. In-depth research takes a long time, so it is recommended to use it in background mode.

screens.outro: Below is the structure of web fetch, code execution, and tool costs.

screens.title: Web Fetch, Code Execution, Tool Costs
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation will appear. Check out both tools and their cost structures one by one.

visual.alt: A horizontal bar where the tool cost is split into tool usage fees and token costs.
labels: Charge based on usage, such as number of searches
Fetched body counts as input token

data.text: web import is a tool that retrieves a specified page and the body content of a PDF, and is used when a URL appears in a conversation; it is not used for general knowledge questions. Code execution takes place safely within sandbox, performing bash commands, file editing, and data analysis. When used in conjunction with web_search_20260209 or web_fetch_20260209 or later versions, code execution is available via Conditions without additional charges. Costs are divided into tool fee and token costs. Gemini documents state that search grounding for Gemini 3 and later models is charged per search query executed by the model, with up to 5,000 queries per month being free. The retrieved document body is counted as input token, so the token cost increases with larger pages retrieved.

terms.tip: This is a tool that reads the pages and PDF text of a specified URL. It is used when a URL appears in a conversation, and is not used in general knowledge questions. URLs that have never appeared in a conversation cannot be retrieved.

This is an environment where code is executed safely and isolated from the outside world. If I implement it myself, the security and dependency management of this environment becomes my responsibility.

If web_search_20260209 or web_fetch_20260209 or later is included in the request, there is no additional charge for code execution beyond the standard token cost. Without these tools, standard rates for code execution apply.

This is a cost based on the number of times the tool is used. For example, search grounding for Gemini 3 and later models is charged per search query executed by the model, with the first 5,000 queries per month being free and $14 per 1,000 thereafter.
The resulting body is counted as an input token. The larger the content you import, the greater the token cost, so it is best to import only the parts you need.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the tools, I'll explain the flow of server tool intervention using an example.

screens.title: Commentary: Flow of server tool intervention in up-to-date information questions
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process by which each exchange rate question is processed in chronological order. Select the right arrow to build up the Search, Calculate, and Answer steps.

visual.alt: A timeline in which search and calculation occur with a single request between the app and the provider server.
labels: Calculate multiplication with search results (execute code)

steps.title: 1. Question
steps.body: A user asks, “How many dollars is 5 million won based on this week’s exchange rate?” This question requires external information, such as the latest exchange rate, and accurate calculation, called multiplication. Neither model alone can reliably resolve them.

steps.title: 2. App sends request only once
steps.body: The app sends just one request with the `web_search` and `code_execution` tools turned on. There is no search integration code or sandbox in the app. The settings that turn the tool on are all the app does.

steps.title: 3. The provider’s server searches.
steps.body: The exchange rate is retrieved from the provider's server based on the model's judgment. If necessary, change your query to search multiple times. This process is invisible to the app and occurs within a single request.

steps.title: 4. Calculate with search results
steps.body: The code runs a calculation that multiplies the exchange rate obtained from the search by 5 million. It is accurate because the model uses the results of running in a sandbox rather than just making up numbers by eye.

steps.title: 5. Final answer with citations
steps.body: The final answer is accompanied by a citation of the source from which the exchange rate was derived. Users can check both the calculation results and the rationale.

steps.title: 6. What the app did
steps.body: The app processed only one response without implementing any intermediate calls. If we had implemented it ourselves, the app would have had to stitch together the search call, result parsing, calculation execution, and source cleanup. The value of server tools lies in reducing this connection effort.

screens.outro: This time, we will compare it to implementing the same function directly.

screens.title: Commentary: Comparing direct implementation, provisioning tools, and change burden
screens.lead: Compare the change burden when instructors implement each function themselves and when they use provided tools. Select the right arrow to fill in rows one by one.

visual.alt: A two-column comparison table comparing direct implementations and provided tools by feature.
labels: Search API replacement, result parsing, and source processing all corrected
Sandbox security and dependency management are my responsibilities.
Leave operation control and cost structure to the provider
Frequently changing and standard functions are provided by tools, and internal data or special rules are implemented directly.

steps.title: If you implement the search yourself,
steps.body: If I need to change the search API to something else, I have to modify all the integration code, result parsing, and source processing. These modifications are repeated each time the search target changes. The burden of change remains on me.

steps.title: Using search as a delivery tool
steps.body: The provided tool can use functions such as dynamic filtering by changing the version value (`web_search_20260209`, etc.). However, you must check whether the model is supported, and the default value of `allowed_callers` varies depending on the version. The burden of changes in search integration and result processing falls on the provider, and I change the version values ​​and settings.

steps.title: If you implement the calculation yourself,
steps.body: It is my responsibility to manage the security and dependencies of the sandbox in which the model runs the code it produces. If there is a problem with the execution environment, accidents may occur. Direct implementation gives you greater control, but also greater responsibility.

steps.title: Using calculations as a tool to provide
steps.body: Provisioning tools instead leave behavioral control and cost structures up to the provider. I cannot decide the execution environment, and the cost follows the structure set by the provider. As the burden decreases, the options also decrease.

steps.title: Judgment criteria
steps.body: For features that change frequently and are standard, for example web search, provisioning tools are beneficial. Functions that require internal data or special rules cannot be replaced by the provider, so you implement them yourself. The question is, is this feature exclusive to my service or is it the same for everyone?

steps.title: mix it up
steps.body: The two methods can be used together. Search and calculation are configured as provided tools, in-house order tracking is configured as a client tool that you implement, and so on. At this time, the step of returning the results of the tool you created is still up to the app.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Who implements it and who takes on the change?
screens.lead: Let's go back to the question we asked at the beginning and try to tie together the judgment criteria for this class.

paragraphs: The initial question was who would bear the burden of implementing the search and computation directly. Server tools are executed by the provider server, so the results are reflected within a single call even if the app does not return tool_result. All three companies offer a line of web search and code execution features, Claude has Web Fetching, and Gemini has URL Context and File Search.

Search grounding helps reduce unfounded answers by linking answers to up-to-date information and sources. Meanwhile, server tools come with a cost. In addition to tool usage fees, such as the number of searches, there is a token cost where the imported content is counted as an input token.

Direct implementation provides greater control, but the burden of maintenance and changes is high, while provided tools provide less burden, but have limited behavior control. A realistic starting point is to divide frequently changed and standard functions into provided tools, and divide functions that require internal data or special rules into direct implementation.

The decision doesn't just happen once. As the service grows, the control limits of the provisioning tool may become an issue, and conversely, as the maintenance burden increases, implementation may be moved directly to the provisioning tool. Either way, the criteria for weighing the burden of change versus control are the same.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: When using server tools, weigh what you gain (less change burden) and what you lose (behavior control, choice of cost structure).

glossary.def: It is a tool that runs on the provider's server and the results are included in the same response.
This feature supports answers with search results and provides sources.
This method filters the imported content through code and puts only the necessary parts into the context.
This is a tool that reads the text of a page or PDF from a specified URL.
It is a tool that executes code in a sandbox to perform calculations and file operations.

misconceptions.fact: There is a tool usage fee and a token fee for imported content. The number of searches and the size of the text retrieved determine the cost.

misconceptions.myth: If you use a server tool, tool_result will never be returned.
misconceptions.fact: The results of the server tools are returned in the same response. However, if you use it with your own client tool, you will again need to take the step of returning the results from that tool.

misconceptions.myth: When web search is turned on, the model always searches.
misconceptions.fact: The model looks at the prompt and searches when it determines it is necessary. Web fetch is also used when a URL appears in a conversation and is not used for general knowledge questions.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Server tools are executed by the provider server, so the results are reflected within a single call even if the app does not return tool_result.
All three companies offer a line of web search and code execution features, Claude has Web Fetching, and Gemini has URL Context and File Search.
Search grounding reduces unfounded answers by linking answers to up-to-date information and sources.
Server tools have tool usage costs, such as number of searches, in addition to the token cost.
Direct implementation provides greater control, but requires a large maintenance and change burden, while provided tools provide less burden but limited behavior control.
